related_questions.question: What do I do if I test positive for E. coli?

text_blocks.snippet: If you test positive for E. coli, it's important to stay hydrated by drinking plenty of fluids, especially if you have diarrhea. Most E. coli infections resolve on their own, but you should contact your doctor if symptoms are severe or persist, particularly if you have bloody diarrhea, a high fever, or signs of dehydration. Avoid taking anti-diarrheal medications, as they can worsen the infection in some cases.
snippet_highlighted_words: stay hydrated by drinking plenty of fluids, especially if you have diarrhea

list.snippet: E. coli infections often cause diarrhea, which can lead to dehydration.
Drink plenty of fluids, such as water, electrolyte drinks, or oral rehydration solutions.
Avoid sugary drinks, as they can worsen diarrhea.

list.title: Mild cases:
list.snippet: If you have mild symptoms like mild diarrhea and stomach cramps that resolve within a day or two, you may not need medical attention beyond staying hydrated.

list.title: Severe cases:
list.snippet: Contact your doctor immediately if you experience:
Bloody diarrhea.
Severe abdominal pain.
Fever over 102°F (38.9°C).
Signs of dehydration (dry mouth, dizziness, decreased urination).
Symptoms of hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), a serious complication.

Do not take anti-diarrheal medications like loperamide (Imodium) or bismuth subsalicylate (Pepto-Bismol) without consulting your doctor, as they can slow down the passage of the bacteria through your system and potentially worsen the infection.
If your doctor prescribes antibiotics, take them exactly as directed.
If you have severe symptoms, you may need to be hospitalized for intravenous fluids or other treatments.

list.title: Handwashing:
list.snippet: Wash your hands frequently with soap and water, especially after using the restroom and before handling food.

list.title: Food Safety:
list.snippet: Practice safe food handling techniques, including thoroughly cooking meats and avoiding unpasteurized products.

list.title: Hygiene:
list.snippet: If you have an infection, avoid preparing food for others and consider staying home from work or school until your symptoms resolve.

text_blocks.snippet: 6. When to Return to Normal Activities:

list.snippet: You can usually return to normal activities when you have been symptom-free for 48 hours and have no signs of infection.
If you have HUS, you may need further testing to ensure your kidneys are functioning properly.

text_blocks.snippet: Treatment for E. coli infections depends on the specific type and severity of the infection. Many E. coli infections, especially those causing digestive symptoms, resolve on their own with supportive care like rest and hydration. However, severe infections or those affecting other parts of the body (like UTIs, meningitis, or sepsis) may require antibiotics. Antibiotics are generally avoided for infections caused by Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) like O157:H7, as they can increase the risk of complications like hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS).
snippet_highlighted_words: Many E. coli infections, especially those causing digestive symptoms, resolve on their own with supportive care like rest and hydration

text_blocks.snippet: 1. Supportive Care (For Most E. coli Infections):

list.snippet: Rest: Allowing the body to recover is crucial.
Hydration: Drinking plenty of fluids, especially oral rehydration solutions, helps prevent dehydration caused by diarrhea and vomiting.
Diet: Eating light, easily digestible foods as tolerated is recommended.

Avoid Antidiarrheals: For STEC infections, medications like Imodium (loperamide) or bismuth subsalicylate (Pepto-Bismol) are generally not recommended as they can slow down the digestive system and potentially increase the risk of HUS.

list.title: Non-STEC Infections:
list.snippet: Antibiotics like ciprofloxacin, azithromycin, or rifaximin may be used for severe or prolonged diarrhea caused by non-STEC strains of E. coli, or for infections outside the digestive tract (like UTIs or sepsis).

list.title: UTIs:
list.snippet: Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, nitrofurantoin, or fluoroquinolones are commonly used to treat E. coli urinary tract infections.

text_blocks.snippet: 3. Hospitalization and Intensive Care (For Severe Complications):

list.snippet: HUS: If HUS develops, hospitalization, potentially in the ICU, may be necessary for blood transfusions and kidney dialysis.

list.title: Antibiotic Resistance:
list.snippet: E. coli can develop resistance to antibiotics, so it's important to choose the right antibiotic based on susceptibility testing.

list.title: Consult a Doctor:
list.snippet: If you have symptoms of an E. coli infection, especially bloody diarrhea, high fever, severe abdominal pain, or signs of dehydration, it's important to seek medical advice promptly.

list.title: Prevention:
list.snippet: Practicing good hygiene, such as thorough handwashing and proper food handling, is crucial in preventing E. coli infections.
